newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein's Adams calls off London meeting.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein's Adams calls off London meeting.

text.p: Gerry Adams, leader of the Sinn Fein political wing of the IRA, cancelled a controversial private visit to Britain's parliament on Thursday and accused the opposition Labour Party of a "McCarthy-style witch hunt".

Adams had hoped to launch his autobiograhy in the historic building on the banks of the Thames River, just three days after British police foiled what they said was an imminent bomb attack by Irish Republican Army guerrillas.
Parliamentary officials cancelled the launch at the weekend but left-wing Labour member of parliament Jeremy Corbyn defied critics and said he would host a private meeting with Adams instead.
Adams said he called off the meeting because the controversy surrounding the visit put Corbyn and another Labour MP, Tony Benn, who was also due to attend in an untenable position.
"I came here as a guest. I have no wish to create difficulties, especially for Jeremy or Tony, or those others who have taken a progressive position on Ireland," he said in a statement.
"The internal Labour Party dispute -- which is in effect a McCarthy-style witch-hunt -- has been a major distraction from the real issues."
Labour party officials had threatened to throw Corbyn out of the party if he went ahead with the meeting. Benn, a former cabinet minister, could have faced similar disciplinary action.
"We utterly condemn his proposed action. If he persists it will be a matter for disciplinary action," Donald Dewar, Labour's chief parliamentary business manager, said on Wednesday.
"It is particularly reprehensible in the light of recent events involving the IRA," Dewar added.

Adams played down the political furore surrounding the visit and said the venue was trivial. It involved an internal dispute with the Labour Party and masked the more urgent problem facing the British and Irish governments -- the breakdown of the peace process in Northern Ireland.
"There are bigger issues, and the biggest issue is how to work out a peace settlement in Ireland," he told reporters.
"I think all of us have to fulfil our responsibilities... for a real peace process."

On Monday police shot dead an IRA suspect in London and seized 10 tonnes of explosives in raids that dealt a severe blow to IRA guerrillas who are battling to oust Britain from Northern Ireland. Five other men were detained in the raids.

Adams was elected MP for West Belfast in the 1980s but never took his seat in the House of Commons. He said he regarded Britain as an occupying power in the province and has refused to take an oath of allegiance to the British monarch.
He has visited parliament several times in the past few years since as a former legislator he cannot be barred.
